prize_parts.citation: For the discovery of GLP-1 as an incretin hormone, its physiology and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My final position is a single-achievement prize for B031 to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. I came into the opening with B046 first and Knudsen in my GLP-1 trio, and I moved in round 1. Nothing in the first-round exchange has moved me back. The decisive reasons are scientific. The chain from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and human physiology, to receptor agonists is unbroken. Independent outcome trials show glycemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit in very large populations. I weigh that demonstrated effect on human disease more heavily than methodological breadth or support counts. The question is not whether the trio is perfect but whether it is the most defensible three-name credit for the discovery arc. I think it is. The citation names the discovery, the physiology and the active form, and also the therapies that followed, so that leaving out Knudsen is not read as a verdict that the drugs were unimportant. TNF blockade (B046) remains my first alternative. It is a clean bench-to-bedside case with a compact pair, and I would support it in a later year, but on breadth and arc it is second to GLP-1 this year.
statement.case_against: The attribution risk has not gone away and I will not minimise it. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide against the Habener group is still unverified from the supplied record, and all six of us are working from recollection. If the committee were shown that her claim is weaker than Habener's, the name list would need rethinking before a vote, and I would then revisit the Knudsen question instead of simply adding a name. Knudsen's acylated analogues are what reached patients, and a prize that is read as honouring only the physiology risks looking as if the pharmacology belongs to nobody. A second part cannot fix that, because a second achievement would force a cut within the three-person cap. I accept that cost. I do not want to dilute a strong single achievement with a weaker second part just to widen the credit.

responses.point: The chair holds that the physiological and chemical core (Holst, Drucker, Mojsov) should take the three slots over industrial drug design, and that the name list should be rethought if Mojsov's priority proves weaker than Habener's.
responses.response: I now agree with that ordering, and I have moved off my opening choice of Knudsen. On your first question I do not think the supplied evidence can settle Mojsov versus Habener, and none of us should claim that it can. Our decision rule should therefore be explicit. We credit Mojsov on the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form and its link to the insulinotropic action that Holst and Drucker documented. We write the citation so that it does not assert exclusive priority over the peptide. We also state in the record that this is a judgment about a contested history, not a finding. On your question about a second part, I see no second achievement strong enough to justify cutting one of the trio. Your later-year placement of B046 I take as a legitimate difference. I read its maturity as a reason it is ready now, not a reason to wait, but I do not rank it above GLP-1.

responses.point: Sandberg argues that if drug development is to be honoured, the better route is a separate prize part and not displacing the identification of the active peptide, and that cytokine-targeted therapy is now a broadly established concept with attribution beyond Feldmann and Maini incomplete.
responses.response: I agree that a discovery prize should not drop the peptide identification in order to reach Knudsen. Where I would push back is on the separate-part idea as a remedy this year. A second part would have to cut the trio or pair Knudsen with a different achievement, and I do not see a principled way to do either. So I would leave the drug-development question to the citation wording and not to the name list. On TNF I accept your point on attribution. Cerami, Vilcek and Kollias are real gaps in the credited pair. I still think a cytokine-targeted class being broadly established is evidence of the achievement, not a discount on it, because it is what the discovery produced. I keep B046 as my first alternative and have not raised it above B031.

responses.point: Perlmann holds that Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is a discovery-stage contribution and that recognising drug design should be a debated choice and not a side effect of dropping the peptide work. He also says the antibody engineering and TNF cloning behind anti-TNF lie outside the credited names.
responses.response: Your framing of drug design as an explicit choice is the right one, and I accept it. I made that choice in the opening by proposing Knudsen, and I reversed it. My reason is that the cap forces a trade-off, and the discovery chain has the stronger claim on the three slots. Your originality objection to B046 is fair and I had understated it: the credited pair does not include the TNF cloning or the antibody engineering. I would hold that against B046 as a first prize, as you do. But I would not call B046 unoriginal, since Feldmann and Maini did the clinical proof of principle that created the field. My remaining disagreement is small. I would keep it as an alternative and not set it aside as a later-year candidate.

responses.point: El-Manira would move to Knudsen as the third name if Mojsov's priority claim were shown not to hold, and ranks optogenetics as an alternative because six credited names make any trio unfair.
responses.response: I agree with your conditional. If it were shown that Mojsov's claim fails, Knudsen would be the natural replacement, and I would accept that. I would add a caution. That would turn the prize towards drug development, so the citation and the other two names would need to be reconsidered together, and I do not think the committee should make that switch on recollection. On optogenetics I remain where I was. The attribution problem is real, but my main objection is that clinical translation is still early, and I weight demonstrated effect on human disease more heavily than the enabling value of a method. I would not use it as the second part of a two-part prize.

responses.point: Linnarsson says he would keep the citation written around discovery of the hormone and its actions, and treats the unfolded protein response (Mori, Walter) as the compact fall-back if the GLP-1 credit cannot be defended.
responses.response: I can accept the citation written around discovery. I have added the physiology and the therapeutic consequence so that the text does not stop at the hormone. As a fall-back, I would not go to B042. I ranked it sixth because the basic discovery is deeply confirmed but its therapeutic payoff is still partial, and Ron and Kaufman fall outside the pair. If the GLP-1 credit failed, the more likely repair is inside B031, with Knudsen or a changed trio, and not a switch to an unrelated candidate. I answer the chair's question on B042 this way: I see no clinical anchor yet that would move it ahead of B031 or B046.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide holds against the Habener group, who are not credited, given that no one can verify the record from the supplied evidence.
Whether leaving out Knudsen can be defended through citation wording alone, or whether the committee would later judge it an under-credit of the therapeutic achievement.
Whether TNF blockade (B046) should be recognised in a later year, and how Cerami, Vilcek and Kollias would be treated alongside Feldmann and Maini.
How durable weight loss, long-term safety and newer indications will affect the description of the achievement.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal issue for any shortlisted ballot, unchanged from round 1. I work in autoimmunity and rheumatology, which is close to B046 (TNF blockade), but my profile documents no personal or institutional tie to Feldmann, Maini or any other shortlisted candidate. My Bergen group-leader affiliation alone does not establish a relationship with anyone on the shortlist. No new disclosure arose from the first-round statements.
